title: A Silence for the Glasshouse
premise: Ada Hartwell has spent two decades as the night librarian of a decaying city conservatory, guarding a secret about her family's fortune and the sister who died for it. When a stranger appears at her father's funeral calling the family by their true, buried name — Okonkwo-Hartwell — Ada discovers her father rewrote his will days before dying, naming an heir nobody expected. As she traces the stranger through the glasshouse archives and her family's corrupted past, she must choose between protecting the loyal cousin who kept her secrets and telling the truth that will shatter them all. In the end, Ada speaks aloud what she has almost said for twenty years, renounces her inheritance, and gives the glasshouse — and the name — back to the city.
about_author: Marguerite Okonkwo is the pen name of a former archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing private papers in institutional libraries across West Africa and northern England. She writes quiet, forensic fiction about families that mistake silence for love.

chapters.title: The Hours After Closing
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. We meet her among the sleeping stacks of the Hartwell Conservatory, where she has worked nights for twenty years, rehearsing sentences she never delivers. Her father's death summons her into daylight for the first time in months. Emotional beat: grief tangled with relief, and the habit of withholding even from herself.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At the funeral, a grey-eyed stranger offers condolences using 'Okonkwo-Hartwell,' a name scrubbed from every record Ada knows. Her cousin Benedict, executor and family loyalist, goes white and ushers the man out. Emotional beat: the first crack — Ada realizes her silence was never hers alone; it was assigned to her.

chapters.title: What the Will Says
chapters.summary: Benedict's POV. Reading of the will: the estate passes not to Ada or Benedict but to a trust 'for the child of Ngozi,' Ada's dead sister — a child no one admitted existed. Benedict burns a letter he was meant to deliver. Emotional beat: loyalty curdling into concealment as Benedict chooses protection over truth.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Palm House
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She finds the stranger, Daniel Okonkwo, waiting in the conservatory's palm house at 3 a.m. He claims to be Ngozi's son, raised abroad on stories of a glasshouse and a grandmother's name. He shows her letters in her father's hand. Emotional beat: vertigo — the family Ada mourned was never the one she lived in.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, interwoven with archival fragments. Flashbacks reveal the night Ngozi died: a fire in the east wing, an insurance payout, a father who chose the company over his daughter and made Ada complicit in the cover story. Emotional beat: shame surfacing; Ada understands why she became a keeper of unread books.

chapters.title: Benedict's Ledger
chapters.summary: Benedict's POV. Benedict discovers Ada meeting Daniel and begins quietly dismantling the boy's credibility — forged documents, he insists, a grifter drawn by the will. But his own ledger shows payments to a private investigator, twenty years of surveillance on Ngozi's lover. Emotional beat: the corruptor's self-justification; he believes he is the family's spine.

chapters.title: The East Wing Reopens
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Following Daniel's letters, Ada breaks into the sealed east wing and finds her father's study preserved like a shrine: the original deed, Ngozi's unsent letter to her baby, and proof the fire was set to destroy evidence of embezzled trust funds. Emotional beat: fury arriving late, sharpened by love for the sister she failed.

chapters.title: Everything the Glass Remembers
chapters.summary: Daniel's POV. Daniel confesses his own deception: the letters are real, but he came not for inheritance alone — his mother died believing this family had erased her, and he wanted an apology more than money. Benedict offers him a settlement to disappear. Emotional beat: the claimant's humanity; truth and ambition indistinguishable even to himself.

chapters.title: The Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Climax. At the trustees' hearing, Benedict presents his sanitized version of the family history. Ada stands, produces Ngozi's letter and her father's confession, and speaks aloud — fully, finally — the account she has rehearsed for twenty years, implicating herself in the silence. Emotional beat: catharsis through public truth-telling; the cost is total.

chapters.title: A Silence, Properly Kept
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, months later. The trust dissolves the estate; the conservatory becomes a public library with a wing named for Ngozi Okonkwo-Hartwell. Benedict leaves without forgiveness; Daniel stays to catalogue his mother's letters. Ada works her last night shift, then locks the door for good. Emotional beat: quiet resolution — goodbye said properly, out loud, at last.
